pronunciation.note: Ḫannaḫannas is Tier 1: the restored form preserves the scholarly citation shape with distinctive Hittite consonants (ḫ/š) that the ASCII form loses; the cuneiform original is written in the Sumero-Akkadian syllabary.

domains.title: ḪANNAḪANNAS — The Grandmother Goddess
domains.subtitle: Birth · Midwifery · Maternal Protection
domains.lead: Ḫannaḫannas is the Hittite "grandmother" goddess, a figure of birth, family, and domestic protection. Her name is a transparent Hittite word meaning "grandmother," and she appears most memorably in the myth of the vanished god Telipinu, where she is sent to search for the angry deity whose withdrawal has blighted the land. As midwife and maternal mediator, she moves between the human household and the divine assembly, easing the passage of new life into the world and the return of absent gods to it.

cards.name: Grandmother
cards.desc: Her name literally means "grandmother," marking her as elder, helper, and wise woman.

cards.name: Midwife
cards.desc: She attends births and protects infants, mothers, and the household.

cards.name: Searcher
cards.desc: In the Telipinu myth she goes out to find the vanished god and restore fertility.

cards.name: Household Guardian
cards.desc: She binds the family together across generations and protects the home.

mythology.lead: Ḫannaḫannas appears in myth and ritual as the one who mends what has been broken by divine anger or human need.

myths.title: The Midwife of the Gods
myths.text: In Hittite birth rituals the grandmother goddess is invoked to protect the mother and child, to open the womb, and to ensure a safe delivery. Her presence turns a dangerous passage into a protected one, and offerings are made to her alongside other deities of birth and destiny.

myths.title: The Search for the Vanished God
myths.text: When Telipinu storms from the assembly and hides himself, the world withers. The Sun Goddess sends Ḫannaḫannas to look for him. The text treats her as the right messenger: a grandmother's persistence and care can coax back even the most angry god.

myths.title: Guardian of the Household
myths.text: Beyond state temples, grandmother figures in Hittite religion protected the household, the storehouse, and the family line. Offerings to Ḫannaḫannas were offerings to the continuity of life itself.

myths.title: Elder of the Assembly
myths.text: As grandmother, she occupies a unique place in the divine assembly: old enough to speak plainly, gentle enough to be heard, and trusted by gods and humans alike to find a way forward.

etymology.derivation: The name is the ordinary Hittite word for grandmother, doubled for affection or emphasis. Its transparency makes it unusual among divine names and underlines the goddess's domestic, familial character.

nameVariations.note: Descriptive English title used in studies of Hittite religion.

originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Hittite cuneiform as 𒄷𒀭𒈾𒄷𒀭𒈾𒀸 — ḫa-an-na-ḫa-an-na-aš. The two ḫ sounds represent the voiceless velar or uvular fricative /χ/, written with the cuneiform ḫ-sign. The Unicode restoration Ḫannaḫannas preserves these distinctive consonants; the ASCII form hannahannas collapses them to plain h.
syncretism:
Ḫannaḫannas belongs to a broad ancient Near Eastern and Mediterranean type: the divine midwife and grandmother.

She can be compared to Roman Bona Dea, Greek Eileithyia, and the Mesopotamian divine midwife Mami/Nintur, all of whom preside over birth and the protection of women. Unlike those figures, however, Ḫannaḫannas is explicitly defined by kinship — she is the grandmother, not merely a birth goddess. This makes her a rare personification of intergenerational care in Bronze Age religion.
culturalLegacy:
Ḫannaḫannas is little known outside Hittite studies, but her role is culturally significant.

She is one of the few Bronze Age goddesses whose primary identity is familial rather than political or martial. Modern scholars of religion cite her in discussions of divine kinship, birth ritual, and the status of elder women in ancient societies. For PuniCodex, her restoration honors the quiet but essential divine work of birth, household, and reconciliation.
extendedMeditation: Ḫannaḫannas teaches that the greatest powers are sometimes the most ordinary. She is not a storm-god or a queen of heaven; she is the grandmother who knows how to find the lost, how to ease a birth, and how to keep a family whole. In restoring her name we restore the dignity of that role: the elder whose patience and care hold the world together.

archaeology: The texts that name Ḫannaḫannas were excavated from the Hittite royal archives at Boğazköy-Hattusa and related sites in central Anatolia, including temple storerooms and administrative buildings within the citadel. The tablets belong to the corpus of Hittite cuneiform literature preserved in the imperial chancery, with duplicates and parallels in Hurrian, Hattic, Luwian, and other Anatolian traditions. Many were written or copied during the Empire period (c. 1400–1180 BCE), though some compositions may descend from older oral or written sources. The clay tablets were baked, either deliberately or by the fire that destroyed the city, which helped preserve them for modern excavation and study.
